messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
HOSPITAL COURSE:

Admission Date: April 29th, 2016
Discharge Date: N/A

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:

Ms. C, a 73-year-old woman with a history of uveal melanoma, was admitted to the hospital for epigastric pain and symptoms of gastric reflux following her second dose of ipilimumab as second line immunotherapy for liver metastases. She also had mild diarrhea with 3–4 loose stools daily. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy were performed to inform further treatment.

FINDINGS:

Esophageal, gastric and duodenal mucosa appeared normal on endoscopic examination without evidence of ulceration or other significant mucosal injury. Gastric biopsies exhibited lymphocytic inflammation surrounding pigmented cells scattered throughout the gastric mucosa. S100 and SOX10 immunostains confirmed multiple microscopic foci of melanoma with tumor associated inflammation resembling gastritis. Flexible sigmoidoscopy and colonic biopsies were normal.

HOSPITAL COURSE AND TREATMENT:

Glucocorticoid treatment was initially deferred as this was considered an appropriate antitumor response, and she received her third dose of ipilimumab. After the 3rd dose, she developed an elevation in her transaminases and bilirubin concerning for checkpoint hepatitis. She was started on glucocorticoids and further immunotherapy was held. Her hepatitis resolved on glucocorticoids. Her gastric symptoms also improved on glucocorticoid therapy consistent with an immune-mediated mechanism.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

Ms. C is advised to continue taking glucocorticoids and report any new symptoms to her healthcare provider. She is recommended to follow-up with her oncologist for further treatment options.
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: [diagnosis section withheld]

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The admission was for epigastric pain and reflux symptoms. Biopsy established that these were caused by gastric metastases of melanoma, which were the finding that explained the admission. Checkpoint hepatitis developed later, after the third dose, and was a separate event. The condition chiefly responsible is therefore a secondary malignant neoplasm of the stomach, which is chapter C. Secondary malignant neoplasm of other digestive organs, including the stomach, is category C78.

CODE: C78
